name: Cruciferous vegetables for estrogen

lead: Men eat broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and similar vegetables, or I3C supplements, to nudge estrogen metabolism and limit estrogenic effects such as softness or chest fat.

Wikipedia describes indole-3-carbinol (I3C), formed from glucobrassicin in these vegetables, as shifting estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic metabolites. Most of that evidence comes from animal and cell studies, and human data on this appearance use are limited and inconclusive.

paras: People add these vegetables to daily meals, often alongside a high-protein cutting diet, and some add I3C or DIM capsules. It is generally treated as a long-term dietary habit.

I3C carries skin and eye irritation warnings in its chemical classification, and Wikipedia advises checking hormone levels before regular supplement use. The vegetables themselves are an ordinary part of the diet.

angle.text: Broccoli, cabbage and I3C supplements are eaten to shift estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic products, for a leaner, less soft look. This is mostly shown in animal and cell studies, with limited human data.

lead: The cruciferous vegetables for estrogen claim holds that eating broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and similar vegetables, or supplements derived from them, shifts estrogen metabolism in a favourable direction, which some men pursue to limit estrogenic effects.

Wikipedia describes indole-3-carbinol (I3C), produced from glucobrassicin in these vegetables, as altering estrogen metabolism toward less estrogenic metabolites, but says most evidence comes from animals and cell studies and human data are limited and inconclusive [1].
infobox: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, kale

paras: I3C forms when glucobrassicin breaks down; it occurs in cruciferous vegetables and is also sold as a dietary supplement [1]. Research focuses on its ability to change how estrogen is processed in the body [1].

Evidence is mainly from lab animals and cultured cells; a review cited by Wikipedia described links between cruciferous vegetable intake and lower breast or prostate cancer risk as limited and inconsistent [1]. In one study, I3C extended survival in lupus-prone mice, with the authors reasoning that I3C alters estrogen metabolism and lupus is estrogen dependent [2]. This is animal research and not about appearance.
Wikipedia notes that because of its effects on estrogen, testing hormone levels is advised before regular supplement use [1].
No studies found. Related work on I3C consists of animal and cell studies, such as a 2009 mouse study in lupus [2].
